researchNotes.title: What T. rex means and when it lived
researchNotes.text: Tyrannosaurus rex means 'tyrant lizard king' in Greek and Latin. The name was given by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905, combining the Greek words tyrannos (tyrant) and sauros (lizard) with the Latin rex (king). T. rex lived during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 68 to 66 million years ago, in what is now western North America. It was one of the very last non-avian dinosaurs to exist before the mass extinction event caused by an asteroid impact wiped out the dinosaurs about 66 million years ago.

researchNotes.title: Size and physical build
researchNotes.text: T. rex was one of the largest land predators of all time. The biggest known specimens, nicknamed Sue and Scotty, measured about 12 to 13 meters (40 to 43 feet) long and stood about 3.7 to 4 meters (12 to 13 feet) tall at the hips. An adult T. rex probably weighed between 5,000 and 9,000 kilograms (5.5 to 10 short tons), roughly as heavy as an African elephant. T. rex walked on two powerful hind legs, balancing its massive skull with a long, heavy tail. Despite its enormous body, many of its bones were hollow, reducing weight without losing strength.

researchNotes.title: The famously tiny arms
researchNotes.text: Compared to its massive body, T. rex had surprisingly short arms with only two clawed fingers on each hand. Despite their small size, the arms were attached to strong muscles and were quite powerful for their proportions. Scientists debate what T. rex used its arms for. Some think the arms helped T. rex push itself up after lying down. Others suggest they were useful for gripping food or holding onto a partner. The arms of young T. rex were larger in proportion to their body than in adults, suggesting they may have become less important as the animal grew and could rely more on its enormous jaws.

researchNotes.title: Skull, teeth, and bite force
researchNotes.text: T. rex had one of the most powerful bites of any land animal ever. Its skull measured up to 1.5 meters (5 feet) long and was wide at the back but narrow at the snout, giving it unusually good binocular vision (the ability to see depth, like humans do). T. rex had about 60 thick, serrated teeth shaped like 'lethal bananas,' the largest measuring about 30 centimeters (12 inches) including the root. Its bite force was three to five times more powerful than a lion's, strong enough to crush bone. Fossilized T. rex droppings contain fragments of crushed bone, confirming that it regularly ate bone along with flesh.

researchNotes.title: Hunter, scavenger, or both?
researchNotes.text: One of the longest-running debates in paleontology was whether T. rex was an active hunter or mainly a scavenger that ate animals already dead. T. rex had excellent senses that support both strategies: a large part of its brain was devoted to processing smells, meaning it could sniff out food over long distances, and its good binocular vision helped it judge distances for hunting. Tooth marks on Triceratops and Edmontosaurus bones prove T. rex ate these animals, and an Edmontosaurus tail fossil with a healed T. rex bite mark shows that at least some prey survived attacks, proving T. rex hunted living animals. Most paleontologists today believe T. rex was both an active predator and an opportunistic scavenger, similar to modern lions and hyenas.

researchNotes.title: Growing up T. rex
researchNotes.text: Like trees, dinosaur bones have growth rings that scientists can count to determine age. Studies of these rings show that T. rex had an incredible adolescent growth spurt. Young T. rex stayed relatively small (under about 1,800 kg) until around age 14, then gained roughly 600 kg (about 1,300 pounds) per year for the next four years -- that is about 4.5 pounds per day! Growth slowed dramatically after age 18. Sue, one of the oldest known T. rex specimens, lived to be about 28 years old, which scientists believe was near the upper end of the species' lifespan. Baby T. rex were about the size of a small turkey and may have been covered in fuzzy feathers, though adults appear to have had scaly skin.

researchNotes.title: Discovery and fossil hunters
researchNotes.text: The first partial T. rex skeleton was found in 1900 in Wyoming by Barnum Brown, a fossil hunter working for the American Museum of Natural History. He found a second specimen in Montana in 1902. These finds were named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905. The most complete T. rex skeleton (about 90% of the bones) was discovered in 1990 by Sue Hendrickson in South Dakota. Named 'Sue' after its discoverer, it took six people 17 days to dig the bones out of the ground. After a legal battle over ownership, the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago purchased Sue at auction for $8.4 million. Museum workers spent over 30,000 hours preparing the skeleton for display.

researchNotes.title: Where T. rex lived
researchNotes.text: T. rex fossils have been found across western North America, in formations stretching from Alberta and Saskatchewan in Canada down through Montana, Wyoming, South Dakota, Colorado, and New Mexico in the United States. During the Late Cretaceous, this region was part of an island continent called Laramidia, separated from eastern North America by a shallow sea. The climate was warm and humid, with lush forests and river floodplains. T. rex shared this environment with other famous dinosaurs including Triceratops, Edmontosaurus (a duck-billed dinosaur), and Ankylosaurus (an armored dinosaur).

researchNotes.title: Senses and brainpower
researchNotes.text: T. rex had a brain about twice as large as those of other big dinosaurs, suggesting it may have been more intelligent. Its brain was especially well-developed in the areas that process smell and vision. T. rex had the best binocular vision of any large theropod dinosaur, meaning it could judge distances extremely well, which would have helped it hunt. A large part of its brain was devoted to processing smells, giving it the ability to detect prey or carcasses over very long distances, much like modern vultures.

researchNotes.title: The extinction of T. rex
researchNotes.text: T. rex disappeared along with all other non-avian dinosaurs about 66 million years ago when a massive asteroid, roughly 10 kilometers (6 miles) wide, slammed into what is now the Yucatan Peninsula in Mexico. The impact caused catastrophic fires, a 'nuclear winter' effect as dust and debris blocked sunlight, acid rain, and dramatic cooling of Earth's climate. About three-quarters of all species on Earth went extinct, including T. rex. However, some small feathered dinosaurs survived and evolved into the birds we see today, making birds the living descendants of the dinosaur family.

researchNotes.title: Famous T. rex specimens
researchNotes.text: Several individual T. rex specimens have become celebrities. Sue (at the Field Museum in Chicago) is the most complete at about 90% and was the most expensive fossil ever sold at auction until Stan surpassed it. Stan (found in South Dakota in 1992, with about 70% of bones recovered) sold for $31.8 million in 2020. Scotty (at the Royal Saskatchewan Museum in Canada) is considered the largest T. rex ever found, estimated at 13 meters long and 8,870 kg. Bucky, discovered by a 20-year-old in 1998, is permanently displayed at the Children's Museum of Indianapolis and was the first T. rex found with a preserved wishbone (furcula), a bone that links dinosaurs to modern birds.

researchNotes.title: Feathers or scales?
researchNotes.text: Since T. rex belongs to the theropod group, which includes many feathered dinosaurs, scientists have debated whether it had feathers. Preserved skin impressions from T. rex and its close relatives show scales, not feathers, on the body. However, baby T. rex may have had fuzzy feathers that disappeared as they grew larger, since large animals do not need insulation as much as small ones. A related large tyrannosaur called Yutyrannus, found in China, did have feathers, but it lived in a much colder climate. If adult T. rex had any feathers at all, they were probably limited to the back, which is the only part of the body where preserved skin has not yet been found.
